title: Interest Is Owed on a Security Deposit
bodyText:
The city requires interest on a residential security deposit (B.R.C. 1981 sections 12-2-5 to 12-2-7). A security deposit is any advance or deposit of money, whatever it's called, whose main purpose is to secure performance of the rental agreement (section 12-2-2), so a pet deposit can count. The interest is simple interest on the full deposit. The city manager sets the rate each December from one-year certificates of deposit and publishes it, and it applies to deposits provided in the next calendar year. For a tenancy of more than one year, figure the interest separately for each year, using the city's list of prior rates and its formula. Under a lease entered into before March 19, 2004, the rate is 5.5 percent a year.

For residential property regulated by state law, the deposit stays the tenant's property. After the tenancy you may keep it or its interest only for actual cause under state law. The city's rule creates a duty to account for the interest, not a fiduciary relationship.

Before the tenant moves in, the written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document you sign and give must say that interest must be paid on the deposit (section 12-2-4(a)(1)(F)). The penalty for violating section 12-2-4 is at most $500 for all violations charged in a single court proceeding.

Return the accrued interest within one month after the lease ends or the home is surrendered and accepted, whichever is later, following state law on returning the deposit and on notice and legality of deductions. Any interest that builds up after that is due when you return the deposit. State law lets a lease allow up to 60 days for the deposit, but the city section doesn't say that extends the month, so pay interest within the month.

If you keep any interest without giving the notice state law requires for keeping a deposit, you lose the right to keep any of the interest. Willfully and wrongfully keeping interest makes whoever holds the deposit (you, or a manager holding it) liable to the tenant for $100 or three times the amount kept, whichever is more, plus reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, if the tenant gave at least seven days' notice before filing. In a tenant's suit under the city's rules the holder must prove that keeping the interest wasn't a violation, and the tenant can bring state and city claims in the same lawsuit. Wrongfully keeping the deposit itself has its own state penalties. A written or oral term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8).

Exception: sections 12-2-5 and 12-2-6 (ownership, return, penalties and burden of proof) don't apply to a deposit paid to a mobile home park for the lease of a mobile home space. State law has the park hold it in a separate trust account and lets the park keep the interest (C.R.S. 38-12-207).
notes: B.R.C. 12-2-2, -4(a)(1)(F), -5 to -8 read; C.R.S. 38-12-103(1)(a). Not decided: whether the general penalty 5-2-4 also applies to 12-2-6(a). City page's 2026 rate and its lease-signing-date reading not adopted: the code ties the rate to the year the deposit is provided. REPLACES the state row's 'no interest is owed'; the state row's pricing-rule interest point isn't repeated. title: A Written Lease and Copies to Each Tenant
bodyText:
If you rent residential property for 30 days or more, enter into a written lease within 30 days after the rental begins (B.R.C. 1981 section 12-2-3). Don't rely on the 30 days: before anyone occupies the rental, you must also have signed and given the tenant a written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document with the city's required disclosures, and must keep an accurate list of the people authorized to live there (section 12-2-4).

Give each tenant a copy of the lease within seven working days after it is fully signed, or within fifteen working days after any tenant signs, whichever comes first. State law separately requires a copy signed by both of you by the seventh day after the tenant signs (C.R.S. 38-12-801), so meet whichever deadline comes first.

Before a summons and complaint under section 12-2-3, the complaining witness or a city peace officer must first request a copy of the lease, and you have five working days from the mailing or delivery of that request to provide it. A written or oral term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8). Violating section 12-2-4 carries at most $500 for all violations charged in a single court proceeding. Section 12-2-3 sets no penalty of its own, so the city's general penalty (section 5-2-4) appears to apply: a fine, and jail only if the violation was intentional, knowing or reckless.

title: No Renting a Building Heated Only by a Solid Fuel Stove
bodyText:
You may not rent out a building if a solid fuel burning device is its sole source of heat (B.R.C. 1981 section 6-9-6). The code's definition of sole source of heat speaks of woodstoves that are the only heating, so treat fireplaces, pellet stoves and other solid fuel devices the same way. A building doesn't count if it has a permanently installed furnace or heating system that uses oil, natural gas, electricity or propane, even one disconnected from its energy source (section 6-9-2). That exception answers only this city rule: state law still requires working heat (C.R.S. 38-12-505).

Any penalty falls on the owner, not the tenant. The fine is up to $100 for a first conviction, $200 for a second and $300 for a third, looking back two years (section 6-9-7).

title: A Working Toilet and Sewage System Is the Owner's Duty
bodyText:
The county's septic system regulations, which cover the whole county including its cities, make the owner of any structure where people live responsible for an adequate, convenient, sanitary toilet and sewage system in good working order (Weld County Code sections 30-1-20 and 30-4-10). Whether that also reaches a home on public sewer isn't clear, because the regulations say they apply to on-site systems (section 30-2-10), so treat it as applying. The regulations cover systems designed for up to 2,000 gallons a day; larger ones need state site approval, design review and a discharge permit.

Sewage or effluent may not be discharged onto the ground or into state waters unless it meets the regulations' minimum requirements or state water quality standards, whichever apply (section 30-4-10). No one may build or maintain a dwelling without adequate sewage disposal; a failed septic system, or a condition the local health agency determines is a public health or safety concern, doesn't count as adequate. Cesspools, pit privies, slit trenches and seepage pits are prohibited. Don't connect more than one dwelling or other unit to the same septic system unless the application and permit specified it (section 30-4-140).

The owner or occupant must let the county in at reasonable times, on reasonable notice, to inspect, test, sample and monitor a septic system; if refused, the county may ask the District Court for an order (section 30-4-60). The county addresses written violation notices to the owner, with a reasonable time to correct. Separately, the owner or occupant must apply for a repair permit within two business days after getting notice that the system isn't working in compliance or is a nuisance or public health hazard, and a permit is needed before any repair; the county may allow emergency use meanwhile (section 30-4-30; C.R.S. 25-10-106(1)(j)). If the health officer finds a system out of compliance, a public health hazard or not repaired in time, then after a hearing on at least 48 hours' written notice the officer may order the owner or occupant to fix it within at most 30 days or stop using it; a petition to the district court must be filed within ten days after the order. On finding a violation, the board of health may assess up to $50 for each day; you may ask the board for a hearing within 30 days after the penalty is assessed (sections 30-4-160 and 30-4-170; C.R.S. 25-10-113). Letting a septic system be used without the required permit, violating a final order, or breaking the state on-site wastewater law, which bars maintaining a dwelling without adequate sewage disposal, is a civil infraction with a fine of up to $100 (C.R.S. 25-10-113 and 18-1.3-503).

City sewer rules not checked. title: Septic Maintenance Is the Owner's Unless a Contract Assigns It
bodyText:
The county makes the owner responsible for maintaining a septic system unless a contract assigns that to a tenant, another party or a public body (Weld County Code section 30-13-10). This applies in the cities too (section 30-1-20). Section 30-4-10 separately requires the owner to ensure a working system and has no exception for a contract.

State law is stricter. Where the work is needed to keep a home habitable, you can move only specific tasks to the tenant, and only for a single-family residence for which you get no government subsidy, in good faith, in a signed writing separate from the lease, with adequate consideration, if the tenant has the skills to do it, and never where it would endanger the tenant's health or safety (C.R.S. 38-12-506). A clause in the lease isn't enough. State habitability law leaves out a few arrangements, unless they were set up to avoid it, such as a cabin in an unincorporated area rented for recreation without public water, heat and sewer service, and premises the occupant uses mainly for agriculture (C.R.S. 38-12-511). Mobile home park spaces are left out too, but park law has its own sewer duties for the landlord (C.R.S. 38-12-212.3).

Cleaning the septic system must be done by a county-licensed systems cleaner (section 30-4-120), and repairs need a county permit (section 30-4-30), whoever is assigned the work.

title: Written Notice of Tenant Rights and Resources
bodyText:
Give tenants the city's written notice of tenants' rights and resources, on a form the city provides or approves (D.R.M.C. section 27-240(b)). The city's form says to use its most current version, at denvergov.org/EvictionHelp. You or your agent must give it when the lease is executed, and again whenever the owner or operator makes a rent demand posted under C.R.S. 13-40-104; give it however you serve the demand. You or your agent must also give it when the Denver Housing Authority or another affordable housing provider sends a notice ending a tenant's subsidy or tenancy.

For a new occupancy of more than 30 days for valuable consideration, no one may move in until you or your agent has provided a copy of an executed written lease, in the time and manner state law sets (section 27-240(a); C.R.S. 38-12-801).

Violations are subject to the city's administrative citations (section 27-240(d)): up to $150, $500 and $999 for a first, second and later citation, unless the Code or the department sets another amount (section 2-293). A residential rental licensee must comply with section 27-240 (section 27-195(d)), so a violation can also bring a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, per day, for which the city may assess a lien on the property (section 27-203), and license suspension, revocation or sanctions (sections 27-240(d) and 27-200).

title: Disclosures Required Before Anyone Moves In
bodyText:
Before anyone occupies a rental as a tenant, lessee or otherwise for valuable consideration, the operator must have executed and given the tenant a written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document containing the following (B.R.C. 1981 section 12-2-4(a)):

- The maximum occupancy levels permitted in the unit, and the names of the people the tenancy agreement allows to live there.
- Notice of the city's rules on nuisance parties (5-3-11), fireworks (5-6-6), trash left against a sign (5-4-12), outdoor furniture (5-4-16), noise (chapter 5-9), weeds (6-2-3), trash accumulation (6-3-3, including 6-3-3(b), which section 12-2-4 describes as the owner's, manager's or operator's duty to keep a trash hauling contract and which now binds the owner and also covers recyclables and compostables), bear-resistant containers (6-3-12), clearing snow from sidewalks (8-2-13) and parking on sidewalks (7-6-13(a)(1)).
- That breaking the city's noise rules, or people living in the unit other than those the agreement lawfully allows, is cause for ending the tenancy.
- That interest must be paid on any security deposit.
- The date and nature of any violations of law in the past 24 months for which the owner, manager or operator received written notice under section 10-2.5-6.
- Notice of the city's cannabis odor rule (now section 5-11-3; section 12-2-4 still cites an old number) and its ban on possessing more than six marijuana plants without a license (6-14-13(a)(6) and 6-16-13(a)(5)).
- The tenant's right to legal representation and the availability of rental assistance, with a complete copy of section 12-2-9(a), using the language in the form created.

The city manager approves a form that satisfies this if fully executed. Using it isn't mandatory if your own document covers everything. Check any form against this list, including the notices of past violations and of the odor rule. Before anyone moves in you must also make, and then keep accurate, a list of the people authorized to live in each unit (section 12-2-4(c)). The penalty is at most $500 for all violations charged in a single court proceeding. The written disclosure requirements don't change anyone's legal rights apart from the duty to disclose. State law still decides when and how a tenancy can be ended. Give the right-to-legal-representation notice again, in the same form, with any notice to quit, demand for compliance or possession, or notice ending Section 8 assistance (section 12-2-9(a)(2)). A term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8).

Dwellings owned by the federal government, the state or their agencies or subdivisions, and state-licensed health care facilities, aren't rental property under the city's definition (section 1-2-1).

title: Heating Must Be Able to Keep 68 Degrees
bodyText:
The city's property maintenance code requires interior space intended for human occupancy to have heating systems, active or passive, able to maintain at least 68 degrees. Portable space heaters don't count (B.R.C. 1981 section 10-2-2, section 602.3 as amended).

An existing structure that complies with all applicable codes in force when it was built is deemed to comply, unless the code official determines that differences endanger the health, safety or welfare of the public or occupants and orders the owner to correct those conditions (section 101.3). Equipment the code requires must be kept in good working order, under the code in effect when the building was legally built, altered or repaired (section 102.2).

The state's heat rules still apply. The state guidance's statement that Colorado sets no minimum temperature is about state law.

The owner, tenant, occupant and their agents are jointly and severally liable for violations. After notice and a chance for a hearing, the city may impose civil penalties of $150, $300 and $1,000 for a first, second and third violation of the same provision, and may revoke the rental license for a violation concerning use of a residential building under that license, and order compliance; the city manager will charge $250 for each investigative inspection. Each day can be a separate offense (section 107.1). If a notice or order is not complied with, the city may also sue, or correct the violation and charge the owner the cost plus up to 15 percent, collected like property taxes if unpaid (section 107.1(a)(6)). Violations can also be prosecuted, with a fine, and jail only for intentional, knowing or reckless conduct (sections 107.1(c) and 5-2-4).

title: Recycling and Organics at Larger Multi-Family Properties
bodyText:
For a building, or part of one, with eight or more dwelling units (the zoning code's multi-unit dwelling), a manufactured home community or a congregate living property, but not residential care under this part of the code, the city's rules apply on and after September 1, 2026 (D.R.M.C. section 48-130). The responsible party must:

- Make sure tenants, residents, employees and contractors have access to on-site recycling and organic material collection.
- Post the notice from the city's Office of Climate Action, Sustainability and Resiliency about recycling and composting.
- Give a copy of that notice to every new tenant.
- Keep records of these requirements.
- Provide recycling and, where applicable, organics information and instructions as city rules require (section 48-134(a)).

The responsible party is the building owner, or the license holder where the property is licensed as a residential rental (or as certain boarding homes or a trailer park), or the association for a condominium or cooperative. It also includes an agent such as a property manager. Required signs and information must be in English and Spanish or picture-only, with universal symbols (section 48-134). A waste diversion plan must exist by the date the rules apply to you, be kept updated and on site, and be produced on request to an enforcement official (section 48-135).

Collection must meet section 48-133: for recycling, at least the materials the statewide producer responsibility program requires; for organics, at least all back-of-house decontaminated food waste; sufficient containers, capacity and pickups; and a licensed hauler or documented self-hauling. City rules can add to or remove from the materials lists. City rules may allow requests for exemption, alternative compliance or shared service (48-133(c)); check whether they do. No variances are allowed (48-137(h)). Someone who starts operating after September 1, 2026 has 30 days after the city license is issued or, if none is required, after taking possession or beginning regular operations (48-133(d)). Violations are unlawful and can bring city citations and licensing action, and a licensee that is the responsible party must give the contact information of the person responsible for compliance and of its haulers with its license application (section 48-137).

title: Billing Tenants for Water From a Master Meter
bodyText:
If the town bills you for water through a master meter serving a building with three or more units or a manufactured home community, and you pass water charges on to tenants, by sub-meters or any other allocation method, on top of the rent, the town's sub-billing rules apply (Frederick Municipal Code section 13-3-319). "Owner" there means whoever holds the billing account with the town. Sub-billing, by you or through a billing agent, is prohibited unless you meet every one of these conditions.

- **Explain it in writing first:** before you sub-bill, give each tenant a detailed written explanation of how charges are allocated. It must include the exact formula for the tenant's share, say whether the tenant pays for any common-area, facility or landscape water and how that share is calculated, and disclose the existence and amount of any administrative fee and required deposit.
- **Pass through only:** the total sub-billed to all units may not exceed what the town billed you, or, if tenants don't pay for common-area, facility and landscape water, what it billed minus that water. Don't bill tenants for late charges, interest, penalties, reconnection fees or deposits you owe the town. You owe the town the whole bill, whatever you collect.
- **Itemize:** show water charges separately from each other and from any other utility you bill. Combining charges, such as billing more for hot water than for cold to recover power costs, is prohibited.
- **Keep 12 months of records:** the town's bills, the allocation formula or sub-meter readings, and a list of each unit's consumption or allocation and the amount billed and collected, plus proof that you gave the written explanation. A tenant or the town may review and copy them, with personal information redacted, on request during normal business hours. If you keep them somewhere else, make them available at the property within five business days of the request. Reviewing is free; you may charge your actual cost for copies.

You may instead include water in the rent. The town rule doesn't cover a single home or a duplex, but the state limits below still do. Putting the town's written explanation in a lease addendum can also meet the state's rule that a ratio-billing method be disclosed in the lease or an addendum, if the disclosure is clear and conspicuous. The town doesn't decide whether your lease allows sub-billing, and doesn't resolve billing disputes.

The town's rule allows some charges that state law forbids, and the state limits still apply. The town lets you charge an administrative fee of up to your actual cost of calculating and collecting the bill and keeping the records (never the cost of the metering equipment), lawful late fees, dishonored check fees and a deposit, each only if disclosed to the tenant in advance and in writing, and lets tenants pay a share of common-area water if it is disclosed. State law forbids charging a tenant more for utilities than the provider charged for the tenant's own unit, except a markup or fee in a written rental agreement of no more than 2 percent of the amount you were billed or $10 a month, not both, or an allocation that meets the state's ratio-billing conditions. It also forbids any fee for late payment of an amount that isn't rent and any fee for maintaining common areas, and it keeps common-area water out of tenants' charges: a tenant's dwelling unit doesn't include common areas, and a ratio allocation must leave common-area and shared-facility costs out (C.R.S. 6-1-737(1)(d)(II), (4) and (4.5), 38-12-801(3)(a)(VI)). In a duplex or triplex where you live in one unit or on the same lot, the 2 percent or $10 allowance doesn't apply, but C.R.S. 6-1-737 still does (C.R.S. 38-12-801(8)). Follow the stricter rule each time: keep any fee within both limits, charge no late fee on a water bill, and leave common-area water out of the tenants' charges. The town's permission to take a deposit doesn't settle whether a separate water deposit fits the state's security deposit rules. In a manufactured home community the town's rules apply, but the state's mobile home park rules differ (the 2 percent or $10 rule doesn't apply there) and aren't covered here.

Each sub-bill presented without meeting these conditions carries a civil penalty of up to $500, with no more than $2,500 for each calendar month of violations. If you are found in violation again in a second action within two years, the maximums double, and the town may shut off water to the master-metered property (section 13-3-319(d)).

title: Furnished Heat Must Reach 68 Degrees From September to April
bodyText:
If you rent a dwelling unit or sleeping unit on terms, written or implied, that you will furnish heat, the town's property maintenance code requires you, as owner or operator, to supply heat from September to April that keeps at least 68 degrees in all habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms (Frederick Municipal Code sections 18-14-10 and 18-14-20(f), amending section 602.3 of the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code). The model code's exceptions to that rule still apply; they aren't covered here.

So in this town, when you furnish heat, the town sets a 68-degree floor; the state guidance's statement that Colorado sets no minimum temperature is about state law. The state's heat rules still apply.

The building official may issue a notice and order to the record owner requiring the correction; the order can also require the building to be vacated. The notice warns that if the repair work isn't started in time, the official will order the building vacated and posted until the work is done, and may have the work done and charge the cost against the property or its owner (section 18-1-60(b)). You may appeal the notice and order in writing to the Building Appeals Board within 30 days of service; if you don't, you give up the right to an administrative hearing (section 18-1-60(b)(1)e). A violation is a noncriminal violation: a fine of up to $1,000, and each day it continues after notice is served is a separate offense (sections 18-1-60(e) and 1-72(a)).

title: Leasing Where Medical Marijuana Would Be Grown Unlawfully
bodyText:
It is unlawful for the owner of a residence or other building to lease it, or any part of it, if the owner knows or reasonably should know that the property will be used to cultivate, produce, possess or process medical marijuana in violation of the town's medical marijuana rules (Frederick Municipal Code section 10-303(a)(11)). When the town has an articulable reason to believe that is happening, it is also unlawful for the owner to refuse a police officer or building inspector access to the part of the building where the suspected activity is located. If an owner or occupant refuses entry, the police may ask the municipal court for a search warrant, and refusing access to an official who presents one is unlawful (section 10-310). The owner or occupant of premises where a patient or caregiver refuses inspection of a grow may also be charged (section 10-308(a)(8)).

Under the town's rules, a lawful medical grow must meet all of these, among others:
- Only a registered patient or licensed primary caregiver, in their primary residence (section 10-303(a)).
- In a home, never more than six plants, no more than three of them mature, per dwelling unit, however many patients or caregivers live there (sections 10-303(a)(1), 10-304(a) and (b), and 10-305(a), (c) and (e)). The code allows more than six plants only in an industrial district, never in a residence (sections 10-304(d) and 10-305(b); Land Use Code section 16-2-40(F)(2)). The Land Use Code allows six plants per person and up to 12 per dwelling (section 16-2-40(F)(1)); the Municipal Code's limit of six per dwelling is the cautious one.
- Not in a garage, a common area of a multifamily or single-family attached property, a yard, shed, greenhouse or other structure outside the residence (section 10-303(a)(3) to (5)).
- No chemical extraction of THC, and no compressed flammable gases such as butane (section 10-303(a)(6) and (7)).
- A locked, fully enclosed area of no more than 150 contiguous square feet in a single-family detached home, or 100 in any other residential structure, closed to anyone but the patient or caregiver and to anyone under 21 (section 10-303(a)(8) and (9)).
- Nothing perceptible from outside the residence by sight, signs, odor or light (section 10-306).

A violation is a criminal violation: up to 364 days in jail, a fine of up to $2,650, or both, and each day is a separate violation. A grow in violation is a public nuisance the town may abate or stop by injunction (sections 10-309 and 1-72(b)). The town may recover its inspection and cleanup costs from the responsible person (section 10-303(a)(10)). Where state law is stricter, the stricter rule governs (section 10-311).

The state guidance on restricting cannabis in the lease still applies. A lease clause banning cultivation is the simplest way to avoid leasing for an unlawful grow; act on any sign that a tenant plans one.

title: Clearing the Public Sidewalk Within 24 Hours
bodyText:
It is unlawful for the owner or occupant of a lot, or an agent in charge of it, to let snow or ice stay on the paved public sidewalk alongside the property more than 24 hours after the last snow or ice accumulated. It is also unlawful to block a street, sidewalk or public right-of-way with snow or ice removed from the lot (Frederick Municipal Code section 11-76).

The duty falls on the owner and the occupant alike, so a lease that makes the tenant clear the sidewalk doesn't remove yours. The library's snow clause covers the areas of the property the tenant uses and excludes areas shared with other residents, so in a multi-unit building it won't cover the public sidewalk. If the tenant is to clear it, add your own clause naming it, and check that it gets done.

The code doesn't designate this violation as criminal, so it is presumed noncriminal (section 10-7(e)): a fine of up to $1,000, and each day is a separate violation (sections 10-7 and 1-72).

title: Unpaid Town Water, Trash and Stormwater Bills Fall on the Owner
bodyText:
The town mails water bills to the record property owner (Frederick Municipal Code section 13-3-321(d)), and its trash and recycling fee and its stormwater fee are charged to the owner of record as the customer (sections 13-300, 13-302, 13-200 and 13-205). A multi-family residence of eight or more units served by a private hauler is exempt from the town trash fee (section 13-302(b)). Water, trash, recycling and stormwater charges for one customer are one debt to the town (section 13-3-320(a)), so an unpaid trash or stormwater fee can also lead to a water shutoff.

If a charge isn't paid when due, the town may use any of these remedies (section 13-3-320(c)):
- Treat it as a lien on the property from the due date, a perpetual charge until paid, and foreclose it.
- Sue for it, with interest, costs and attorney fees as allowed by law.
- Certify it to the county, with an assessment fee, to be collected like property taxes.
- Shut off water after sending the record owner a written notice.

Unpaid water bills and assessments become liens on the property (section 13-3-321(g)). Every fee or charge owed to the town is a prior, perpetual lien from its due date, and the town may withhold or revoke permits, certificates, approvals or licenses while one is delinquent (section 1-76).

Water bills are due by the 15th. When an account is 60 or more days past due, a written notice is mailed by the 20th. An amount 30 or more days past due that isn't paid by 5:00 p.m. on the late-notice due date, the Tuesday before the first Wednesday of the month, means the water is turned off (section 13-3-321(d)). The shutoff notice section states the date slightly differently (the first Tuesday of the month after the notice, section 13-3-320(c)(4)a); the safe course is to pay every bill by the 15th. Payments go first to delinquent amounts, then late fees, then restoration fees, then current charges (section 13-3-320(b)). Once water is off, it isn't restored until all past-due and current charges, the restoration fee and any other fee, assessment or charge the town has imposed under its code or made a lien on the property, such as inspection and testing fees, are paid in full (section 13-3-320(c)(4)d). If everything due is paid by 5:00 p.m. on a business day, water is restored by the next business day (section 13-3-321(d)).

If the town shuts off water at a rented home, the home lacks running water under the state's habitability law, a condition rebuttably presumed to materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety (C.R.S. 38-12-505(4)(c)), so at the tenant's request you must provide a comparable unit or a hotel room within 24 hours at no cost to the tenant (C.R.S. 38-12-503(4)(a)(II)). Willfully causing the termination of running water is unlawful exclusion, with damages of at least the tenant's actual damages plus the higher of three times the monthly rent or $5,000 (C.R.S. 38-12-510); whether letting a bill go unpaid counts as willful isn't settled by the statute, so don't let it happen. The state guidance on utility liens and on accounts in your name still applies.

Whether a tenant may hold the town account is not addressed by the code. Drafted 2026-11-25 from sections read by Claude Code; round 1 independent check run. title: Weeds Over Eight Inches, Brush and Rubbish
bodyText:
The owner, lessee, agent, occupant and anyone else in possession or control of a lot, occupied or not, must not permit weeds taller than eight inches, any brush, or any accumulation of rubbish on the lot or along the sidewalk, street or alley next to it (Frederick Municipal Code sections 7-33(a) and (b) and 7-34). Weeds are volunteer growth of grass and other plants, including noxious weeds and their cuttings, but not a cultivated, planned and maintained landscape or garden; brush is woody shrubs outside a planned and maintained landscape, plus tree and bush cuttings; rubbish includes waste, leaves, grass cuttings and trimmings, manure, ashes, cans, bottles and discarded construction materials (section 7-31). Noxious weeds have their own rules (sections 7-33(d) and 7-39).

Nobody may put rubbish, weeds or brush on a street, alley or any property except in proper containers for collection or with the town's approval. Refuse containers must stay covered, off the street, curb and sidewalk, and out of public view except on collection day (section 7-32).

The duty falls on you and your tenant alike, so a lease that makes the tenant do the yard work doesn't remove yours. If the town finds a violation, it may give the owner and the tenant or other person in possession ten days, or longer if it decides, to correct it. If it isn't corrected, the town may enter, do the work, and assess the actual cost plus an administrative fee against the owner and the tenant, who owe it jointly and severally. The assessment is due 30 days after notice, and if unpaid the town may certify it to the county treasurer, with a collection penalty, to be collected like taxes (section 7-35). The town may also prosecute: these are noncriminal violations with a fine of up to $1,000 (sections 7-36 and 1-72(a)).

The state guidance on nuisance fines and abatement costs still applies, including your right to recover your costs from a tenant who caused the problem.
notes: F.M.C. 7-31 to 7-36 read whole; 1-72 read. 7-39 (noxious weeds) and 18-14-20(d) (IPMC 302.4, same 8-inch limit) not drafted separately. 'Each day a separate violation' not stated: 10-7(b) says so unless otherwise provided; not repeated here. Drafted 2026-11-25 from sections read by Claude Code; independent check not yet run.

title: Removing Graffiti Within Seven Days of Notice
bodyText:
Graffiti on property that is visible to public view is a public nuisance (Frederick Municipal Code section 10-76(e)). The town may give the property owner written notice to remove it within seven days of the date of the notice, or another time it considers reasonable (section 10-76(g)). For this section "owner" includes anyone leasing, occupying, or having the right to possession or control of the property, so the notice may go to your tenant or to you.

If the graffiti isn't removed in time, the town may enter the property and remove it (section 10-76(h)). The cost, plus 5 percent for inspection and administrative costs including attorney fees, is assessed against the owner and the lessee, agent, occupant or other person in possession or control, who owe it jointly and severally. It is due 30 days after notice, and the town may send an unpaid amount to collections (section 10-76(i)).

The state guidance on nuisance fines and abatement costs still applies.
notes: F.M.C. 10-76 read whole, 10-9 and 1-72 read. Penalties in 10-76(k) apply to violations of the section (defacing, materials); whether failing to remove after notice is itself a violation is not stated, so no penalty is given here. title: Repairing Water Leaks Within Ten Days of Notice
bodyText:
Plumbing, pipes, water meter connections and irrigation systems must be kept free of leaks. After the town issues a notice of violation, the property owner must shut off or repair a leak as soon as practicable, and in no event more than ten days from the date of the notice; a leak that continues past ten days is a public nuisance (Frederick Municipal Code section 13-3-326(b)(1)).

No customer or owner may waste water. Watering a lawn or landscaped area, or a patio, driveway, vehicle or other surface, so that water pools or flows steadily into storm drains or onto other property, streets, sidewalks or driveways is water waste, and so is ignoring a leak order. It must be fixed within the same ten days of a notice (section 13-3-326(b)(2)). If the town engineer reasonably finds extreme water waste, the town may install a flow restrictor at the owner's cost, added to the owner's utility bill, or shut off water to the property (section 13-3-326(b)(3)). The board of trustees or the town manager may also impose mandatory water use restrictions from the town's Water Shortage Contingency Plan at any time (section 13-3-327).

The repair duty is the owner's. The library's landscaping clause asks the tenant to report leaks promptly, which helps you meet the ten days.
